title: Investigating Students’ Preferences for AI Roles in Mathematical Modelling: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how students perceive different AI roles during mathematical modelling and whether those roles affect learners’ confidence, perceived helpfulness, ease of interaction, and preference rankings. The authors are motivated by a broader question in AI in education: not just whether AI can help, but which pedagogical persona is most suitable for supporting the iterative and cognitively demanding process of mathematical modelling.

The intervention compared five AI roles: Tutor, Teaching Assistant, Peer Student, Struggling Student, and Excellent Student. A no-assistance baseline task was also included. All AI responses were generated with GPT-based models and constrained by role-specific prompts. The study used a within-subjects, counterbalanced randomized design in which 26 university students each completed one baseline modelling task and five further modelling tasks, each with a different AI role. Participants were non-STEM undergraduates or university students with no university-level mathematics coursework, recruited online in Hong Kong SAR / China-related university settings.

Results showed that students strongly preferred competent, supportive AI roles over the Struggling Student role, which was rated worst across preference, confidence, helpfulness, and ease of interaction. Among the four competent roles, there were no statistically significant differences in most outcomes, suggesting that students valued competence and support more than a specific instructional style. The only notable subgroup difference was that students with higher design thinking scores preferred the Teaching Assistant role more than lower-scoring peers. The paper concludes that AI for mathematical modelling should prioritize accurate, supportive, and pedagogically coherent behavior, while cautioning that low-quality or confused AI personas are likely to undermine the learning experience.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized counterbalanced within-subjects study, but it does not directly compare an AI intervention against a non-AI baseline on a learning outcome. The main results are preference and perception measures plus correlational/SEM analyses, so it provides useful evidence but not high-causal evidence for educational effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear preference and usability advantages for competent AI roles over a low-quality AI persona, but it does not report achievement gains or other direct educational impact outcomes. Because the main findings are perceptual rather than performance-based, the practical impact is promising but unclear.

interventions.use_case: GPT-based AI role-play in mathematical modelling tasks, where the same model was prompted to act as a Tutor, Teaching Assistant, Peer Student, Struggling Student, or Excellent Student to guide students through modelling problems via short dialogue turns.

finding.finding_summary: This RCT did not measure learning gains on a posttest; instead, it compared how students perceived different AI roles during mathematical modelling tasks. Across n=26 participants completing six tasks, the study found strong preferences for competent AI roles over a Struggling Student role, with the Tutor role ranked best (M=2.35, SD=1.02) and the Struggling Student role worst (M=4.42, SD=1.17).
finding.measure: AI role preference rankings and perceived task confidence/helpfulness/ease during mathematical modelling tasks
finding.effect_size: r=0.85 for Tutor vs Struggling ranking difference; r=0.80 Excellent vs Struggling; r=0.67 Peer vs Struggling; r=0.57 TA vs Struggling; Friedman χ2(4)=28.83, 24.85, 32.63, 36.43
finding.std_deviation: SDs reported for role ratings/rankings: Tutor 1.02, Excellent 1.30, Peer 1.19, TA 1.41, Struggling 1.17

finding.finding_summary: Students reported significantly higher task confidence, perceived helpfulness, and ease of interaction with competent AI personas than with the Struggling Student role. For example, task confidence was highest with Excellent Student (M=3.69, SD=1.19) and Tutor (M=3.65, SD=1.16) and lowest with Struggling Student (M=1.88, SD=1.24), with Friedman tests showing significant role effects (χ2(4)=24.85, 32.63, 36.43; all p<.001).
finding.measure: Task confidence, perceived AI helpfulness, and ease of interaction (Likert scales)
finding.std_deviation: Tutor confidence SD=1.16; Excellent confidence SD=1.19; Peer confidence SD=1.14; TA confidence SD=1.39; Struggling confidence SD=1.24

finding.finding_summary: Baseline design thinking and computational thinking were positively associated with mathematical modelling self-efficacy, suggesting these durable skills matter for modelling confidence. In PLS-SEM, design thinking predicted MMSE strongly (β=0.730, p<.001, f2=2.288) and computational thinking also predicted MMSE (β=0.300, p<.001, f2=0.387), with the model explaining 80.8% of variance in MMSE (R2=0.808).
finding.measure: Correlations among CT/DT subdimensions; PLS-SEM predicting mathematical modelling self-efficacy
finding.effect_size: β=0.730 for DT→MMSE; β=0.300 for CT→MMSE; R2=0.808; f2=2.288 and 0.387
